papers.title: Discrete truncated Wigner approximation of the quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising model
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34004v1

summary.one_liner: This paper tests whether the discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA), a semiclassical method for spin dynamics, captures the Kibble-Zurek scaling of the transverse-field Ising model's quantum phase transition in one to three dimensions and for all-to-all coupling.
summary.plain: The study looks at a magnet made of tiny quantum spins that is slowly or quickly tuned through a point where it switches from disordered to ordered. The authors test a cheaper approximate simulation method (DTWA) against more exact quantum Monte Carlo results. They report that the method fails on a one-dimensional chain, locates the onset of order reasonably well in square and cubic lattices, but does not reproduce the universal scaling of the transition there; for all-to-all coupling it tracks the exact order growth.
summary.why: Large quantum systems are hard to simulate exactly, so knowing where a cheap approximation can be trusted matters for researchers using it. The text suggests the method's reliability grows with the number of neighbours each spin interacts with, but this is a finding about one model and one method, not a general verdict.
summary.background:
- Spin: a tiny quantum magnet, which can point up or down.
- Transverse-field Ising model: a standard model of spins on a lattice that compete to align, with a field that flips them sideways; it has a quantum phase transition between disordered and ordered states.
- Quantum phase transition: a change in a system's collective state driven by quantum effects at zero temperature, rather than by heat.
- Ramp: slowly or quickly changing the control parameter (the field) through the transition.
- Kibble-Zurek mechanism: a theory predicting how many defects or how much disorder remains after a transition, depending on ramp speed, following universal power laws (the "exponents").
- Discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA): a semiclassical method that treats quantum spins as classical ones with random initial states to approximate dynamics cheaply.
- Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC): a numerical method using random sampling to simulate quantum systems accurately, used here as the reference.
- Effective temperature: a classical thermal temperature that a relaxing simulation settles into, used to explain DTWA's failure in 1D.

papers.abstract: The discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA) has been a workhorse for large-scale spin dynamics, but whether it captures dynamics across a quantum phase transition has not been tested systematically. In this work, we use the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) to study the quantum phase transition with DTWA from one to three dimensions and with all-to-all connectivity, using slow linear ramps and fast ramps. We find that DTWA cannot capture the dynamics on the one-dimensional chain, and that its behavior is consistent with classical thermalization, in which its classical spins relax toward a thermal state at a finite effective temperature that does not vanish for slow ramps, while a one-dimensional chain cannot order at any finite temperature. For square and cubic lattices, in contrast to the chain, DTWA builds order, and the order sets in close to the quantum critical point found by quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, its correlations do not grow with the Kibble-Zurek exponents, so DTWA captures the onset of order but not the universal dynamics of the transition. For all-to-all coupling, DTWA follows the exact growth of the order parameter along the entire ramp. Our results suggest that DTWA becomes more reliable as each spin interacts with more partners, and that beyond one dimension it can indicate where a quantum phase transition lies but cannot capture its critical scaling.

papers.title: From Spin Glass Theory to Optimization in High Dimensions and Modern Artificial Neural Networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34713v1

summary.one_liner: A tribute chapter reviewing how replica symmetry breaking and cavity methods from spin-glass theory have been applied to combinatorial optimization, random satisfiability, survey propagation, and the geometry of solution spaces in neural networks.
summary.plain: This is a review chapter honoring physicist Giorgio Parisi, looking at how ideas he helped develop for disordered magnets (spin glasses) have spread into computer science problems and modern neural networks. It walks through classic puzzles such as matching and the traveling salesman problem, then discusses how the shape of the set of good solutions relates to how hard a problem is to solve and how a network learns. The text is a survey of established ideas and examples rather than a report of one new result.
summary.why: The chapter links a body of physics theory to practical questions about why some optimization and learning problems are hard and others are easy to solve. Its link to neural network training is of current interest, though the provided text only outlines these connections and does not give specific quantitative findings.
summary.background:
- Spin glass: a magnet with randomly mixed friendly and hostile interactions, so it cannot settle into one simple arrangement.
- Replica method: a mathematical trick from physics for averaging over many random systems at once.
- Replica symmetry breaking (RSB): Parisi's refinement, where the set of low-energy states splits into many separated clusters.
- Cavity method: an approximation technique for estimating how a large random system behaves when one piece is removed.
- Combinatorial optimization: finding the best option among a huge number of discrete choices, e.g. shortest route for a traveling salesman.
- Survey propagation: a message-passing algorithm for hard satisfiability problems, derived from the cavity approach.
- Overparameterized model: a neural network with more adjustable weights than training examples.

papers.abstract: This chapter pays tribute to Giorgio Parisi by reviewing the influence of his work on spin glasses and replica symmetry breaking (RSB) on combinatorial optimization and artificial neural networks. We first introduce replica and cavity methods through the matching and traveling salesman problems, before discussing random satisfiability and the development of survey propagation. We then examine applications to neural networks, emphasizing the connections between the geometry of solution spaces, computational hardness, and learning. Particular attention is given to rare regions of high local entropy and their role in algorithmic accessibility. Examples involving overparameterized models and asymmetric recurrent networks illustrate how these ideas connect constrained optimization and inference with concepts developed in spin-glass theory.

papers.title: Parametric neural-network wavefunctions across a bosonic phase transition
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33150v1

summary.background:
- Bosons: particles (such as some atoms) that can share the same quantum state, unlike electrons.
- Wavefunction: the mathematical function that gives the full quantum description of a system.
- Phase transition: an abrupt change in a material's state, such as melting or freezing, here between flowing (superfluid) and ordered (crystal) forms.
- Hamiltonian parameter: a tunable setting in the system's energy rules, here the strength of interactions.
- Variational Monte Carlo: a method that tunes an approximate wavefunction using random sampling to lower its energy.
- Neural-network wavefunction: using a neural network as a flexible, trainable guess for the wavefunction.
- Attention: a neural-network mechanism that lets each part of the input weigh other parts, widely used in modern AI models.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces Boseformer, an attention-based neural-network ansatz that is trained over a Hamiltonian parameter to represent bosonic wavefunctions across a superfluid-to-crystal quantum phase transition in 2D bosons with 1/r^3 repulsion.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how a gas of particles that follow bosonic quantum rules behaves as it shifts between a flowing superfluid state and an ordered crystal state. The authors build a single neural network that describes the quantum wavefunction (the mathematical object encoding the system's state) for many strength settings of the interaction at once. Once trained, it can be used across the transition without retraining for each setting.
summary.why: Describing phase transitions in quantum matter is computationally hard, and a model that works across a range of parameters without retraining could reduce that cost. The text is a short abstract, so it does not show how accurate the results are or how the method compares with existing approaches, and its wider significance is not yet established.

papers.abstract: We propose Boseformer, a universal attention-based neural-network architecture for representing the wavefunctions of particles with bosonic quantum statistics, including superfluid and crystal phases. The model is trained to generate the wavefunction as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across the quantum phase transition between these phases. Once trained with variational Monte Carlo optimization, it can serve as a foundation model describing the phase transition without the need to retrain it for individual parameter values. We demonstrate our method on a system of two-dimensional bosons with $1/r^3$ repulsive interaction.

papers.title: Polar Streams through Active Condensation in Flocks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33007v1

summary.background:
- Active matter: systems whose units consume energy to move on their own, such as colloids, cells or animals.
- Janus colloid dimers: pairs of micron-scale particles with two faces of different chemistry, which self-propel when driven (here, the experimental model).
- Flocking: particles aligning their directions so the group moves coherently; the Toner-Tu equations are the standard continuum description.
- Motility-induced phase separation: self-propelled particles bunch together into dense clusters even without attraction between them.
- Polar vs. nematic order: polar order means all particles point the same way; nematic order means they share an axis but may point either way.
- Coarse-graining: replacing individual particles with smooth density and orientation fields to derive a hydrodynamic theory.
summary.one_liner: Experiments on self-propelled Janus colloid dimers, backed by simulations and coarse-grained hydrodynamic theory, show that flocks can phase-separate into elongated polar streams via an "active nematic condensation" mechanism in which denser regions gain stronger polar and nematic order that draws in more particle flux.
summary.plain: Researchers studied tiny self-propelled particles that move together as a group, called a flock. They found that the flock can split into dense, elongated streams that move along their long axis, instead of the sideways bands usually seen near the point where flocking begins. The text attributes this to a feedback loop: denser parts of the flock align more strongly, which pulls in even more particles.
summary.why: The paper proposes that flocking and clustering can work together rather than only compete, and that nematic order (alignment without a preferred direction, like rods lying side by side) can shape flocks, which the standard Toner-Tu flocking equations do not include. Its wider relevance to natural or engineered swarms is suggested by the authors as a generic mechanism, but the text itself does not test that beyond this system.

papers.abstract: Two of the most paradigmatic phenomena in active matter are flocking, where particles align to move collectively, and motility-induced phase separation, where self-propulsion causes particles to condense even without attractive interactions. Here, using experiments on self-propelled Janus colloid dimers, we show that flocks can phase separate to form polar streams. These structures are elongated dense clusters of particles that flock along the stream's long axis, in contrast to the well-known transverse bands that form close to the flocking transition. We use particle-based simulations and hydrodynamic theory obtained through coarse-graining to identify the underlying mechanism, which we call active nematic condensation: Denser regions of the flock develop stronger polar and hence nematic order, which leads to further particle fluxes into the dense region. These results reveal a generic mechanism whereby flocks can condense into streams. Our findings uncover that flocks can be shaped by nematic order, which is usually not accounted for in the standard Toner-Tu equations. More broadly, our work shows that collective motion and phase separation can not only coexist but also cooperate in active matter.

papers.title: Statistical mechanics of noisy collisions in active matter: Dyson-Landau theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30910v1

summary.background:
- Kinetic theory: describes many-particle systems by a distribution function evolving under collisions.
- Landau collision integral: the standard kinetic equation for weakly interacting particles.
- Fokker–Planck equation: describes diffusion driven by random noise.
- Dyson expansion: a perturbative series for corrections to a propagator (the evolution operator of a system), here applied to noisy dynamics.
- Active matter: systems whose components consume energy to self-propel, such as flocks or motile cells.
- Dry aligning active matter: self-propelled particles that align their directions without a surrounding fluid.
- Weak noise / high activity: the limit where the random forcing is small relative to the deterministic dynamics.
- Non-analytic and logarithmic corrections: terms that cannot be written as simple power series in the noise strength, indicating subtle long-time interaction effects.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the Landau kinetic equation for weakly interacting particles to include microscopic noise, via a Dyson expansion of the noisy free propagator, and examines how noise and collisions interact in active matter models.
summary.plain: Many models of self-propelled or "active" particles, such as flocking animals or motile cells, describe motion with random jitter at the smallest scale, which standard physics derivations do not naturally produce. The authors ask how to build this kind of random noise properly into the kinetic theory that describes how particles collide and exchange momentum. They find that a common shortcut is correct at leading order in one case, but that for aligning particles and for noise acting only during collisions, the corrections are unusual: they are non-analytic, odd in the coupling strength, and their sign depends on the direction of alignment, which agent-based simulations support.
summary.why: The work addresses a foundational question about whether common modelling shortcuts for active matter are justified from microscopic dynamics. It may matter for the theory of flocking and active fluids, but the text alone does not show how broadly the results apply beyond the minimal models studied.

papers.abstract: Active systems and other coarse-grained descriptions are often modeled by generalized dynamics, effective equations of motion that are not bound by the constraints of genuinely microscopic physics. In particular, these equations are generally stochastic on the smallest resolved scale. This poses a challenge to first-principles statistical physics, which usually derives emergent noise on larger scales from deterministic interactions. Here, we show how to systematically incorporate microscopic noise into kinetic theory in the limit of weak noise, i.e., high activity. By means of a Dyson expansion of the noisy free propagator, we derive the leading correction to the Landau kinetic equation for weakly interacting systems. We find that the common practice of combining a deterministic collision integral with the diffusive terms of the Fokker--Planck equation is the correct leading order. For dry aligning active matter, however, the corrections are non-analytic in the noise strength, as nearly parallel particles interact for arbitrarily long times. For noise that acts only during interactions, a minimal model of stochastic interactions, noise and collisions do not decouple: the leading corrections are odd in the coupling strength, partly logarithmically enhanced, and amount to an orientation-dependent effective noise strength. Agent-based simulations confirm the predicted dependence on the sign of the coupling. Even in this minimal model, the effect of noise on collisions can thus not be inferred from symmetry alone.

papers.title: Trajectory arclength reveals thermodynamic criticality
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30053v1

summary.background:
- Phase transition: a qualitative change in a system's collective state, such as magnetization appearing below a critical temperature.
- Thermodynamic limit: the idealized case of infinitely many particles; sharp non-smooth features (non-analyticity) appear only there.
- Hamiltonian: the function giving a system's energy, which determines how its particles move over time.
- Mean-field model: a simplified model in which each particle interacts equally with all others, making it analytically tractable.
- Arclength: the total length of a path traced through the system's state space.
- Lagrangian descriptor: a diagnostic computed by integrating a quantity along trajectories, used to probe dynamical behavior.
- Finite-size correction: the deviation from the infinite-system limit that appears in finite systems, here scaling as N^(-1/2) with N the number of particles.
summary.one_liner: For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, the equilibrium-averaged arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories, written as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, develops a kink at the phase transition, with a leading finite-size correction scaling as N^(-1/2) and an analytically derived prefactor.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a phase transition, the sudden change a system undergoes such as water freezing, leaves a visible trace in how far its tiny constituent particles travel along their paths of motion. The authors measure the length of those microscopic paths in a simple model of many interacting spins and find a sharp corner (a kink) right at the transition. They also derive how the difference from the infinite-system limit shrinks as the system grows, and report that simulations with up to 10^5 degrees of freedom match these predictions.
summary.why: The appeal is that the signal is computed from trajectories alone, without tangent-space evolution or a pre-chosen order parameter, which the text presents as a simpler route to detecting criticality. Whether this generalizes beyond the mean-field model studied here is not addressed in the text.

papers.abstract: Thermodynamic criticality arises at continuous phase transitions, where collective interactions produce non-analytic behavior in equilibrium thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit. We show that this criticality also leaves an analytically predictable signature in the arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories. For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, we derive the thermodynamic limit of the equilibrium-averaged arclength, formulated as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, and demonstrate that it develops a kink precisely at the phase transition. We trace this non-analyticity to spontaneous magnetization and derive the leading critical finite-size correction, scaling as $N^{-1/2}$ with an explicit analytical prefactor. Simulations with up to $10^5$ degrees of freedom confirm both predictions without adjustable parameters. Requiring neither tangent-space evolution nor prior specification of an order parameter for its computation, trajectory arclength provides a simple, quantitative link between microscopic Hamiltonian motion and collective thermodynamic criticality.

papers.title: Large deviations, effective dynamics, and dynamical phase transitions in random maps
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26704v1

summary.background:
- Random maps: systems that update in discrete time steps, with each step including some randomness.
- Large deviation theory: the mathematics of how improbable averages over time behave, typically with probabilities decaying exponentially.
- Time-averaged observable: a quantity averaged over a long trajectory, such as how often a state is visited.
- Doob transform: a reweighting of a random process that changes its probabilities so that a chosen rare event becomes the likely outcome.
- Tilted operator: a modified transfer operator whose leading eigenvalue and eigenfunctions encode the rate of rare events.
- Dynamical phase transition: an abrupt change in the typical behavior of a trajectory as a control parameter (here, the size of the deviation being studied) varies.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the Doob transform and spectral large-deviation methods from deterministic chaotic maps to random maps, to build effective dynamics for rare trajectories and to characterize dynamical phase transitions.
summary.plain: The paper studies unusual, rare patterns of behavior over long stretches of time in simple systems that evolve in discrete steps with added randomness. Such patterns are exponentially hard to observe by just running the system normally. The authors show how to build a modified version of the dynamics in which these rare behaviors become typical, so they can be reproduced directly, and they use spectral methods to see when the system switches between different behavioral regimes.
summary.why: Rare fluctuations and sudden switches between behavioral regimes are central questions in statistical physics, and the framework could help study them in a wider class of systems. The text itself does not indicate specific applications beyond random chaotic maps, so the broader reach is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Large deviation theory provides a natural framework to characterize rare fluctuations of time-averaged observables in deterministic and stochastic systems. Building on previous results for deterministic chaotic maps, here we extend the Doob transform to random maps, constructing an effective dynamics in which rare events become typical. This makes it possible to directly reproduce the dynamics of rare trajectories that are exponentially difficult to sample under the original dynamics. We further apply spectral large-deviation methods to characterize dynamical phase transitions in random maps. The spectral structure of the tilted operator provides insight into the mechanisms underlying these transitions and, in particular, allows us to identify the appropriate initial states that select one dynamical phase or another. Our results extend the connection between large deviation theory, spectral methods, and effective dynamics to random chaotic maps, providing a general framework to study rare events and dynamical phase transitions in these systems.

papers.title: Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network
papers.label: arXiv:2610.03169v2

summary.background:
- Simplices: building blocks of a shape or network: points (dimension 0), edges (1), triangles (2), and higher.
- Simplicial complex: a collection of such blocks glued together; it can represent group interactions, not just pairwise links.
- Cochain: an assignment of numbers (features) to the blocks of a given dimension; node-based variables are 0-cochains.
- Boundary operators and Hodge Laplacians: standard tools that move information between neighbouring dimensions of a complex.
- Cup and cap products: operations from algebraic topology that combine features across dimensions, allowing jumps of more than one dimension.
- TopoBench: a benchmark suite for topological neural networks.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes the Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network (CCNN), which uses cup and cap products from algebraic topology to move signals between simplices of different dimensions in one layer and learns node-level features via many-body (e.g. triangle) interactions, validated on TopoBench datasets against other simplicial complex networks.
summary.plain: Many machine-learning models built on shapes or networks of connected parts can only pass information between neighbouring levels of structure, such as points to lines or lines to triangles, one level at a time. This paper proposes a new model that uses mathematical operations called "cup" and "cap" products, which let information jump across more than one level in a single step. The authors test it on standard benchmark datasets and report that it performs competitively with other existing models of this kind.
summary.why: The work targets a stated limitation of current topological deep learning, namely that signals can only be raised or lowered one dimension per layer, so it may matter for modelling group interactions in data. The text reports only competitive benchmark performance, not superiority, so the practical gain is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Topological Deep Learning (TDL) is designed to learn features associated not only with nodes but also with edges, triangles and higher dimensional simplices. However, most TDL approaches, being based on boundary operators and Hodge Laplacians, have the limitation that features and signals cannot be lifted or lowered across more than one dimension per layer. To overcome this limitation, in this work, we propose the adoption of the cup and cap products. Specifically, we formulate the Cup and Cap Topological Neural Network (CCNN), a topological deep learning architecture designed to learn node-based variables (or 0-cochains) by taking into account their many-body interactions (e.g. triangles) present in the data. We validate CCNN by assessing its performance on the TopoBench datasets, demonstrating its competitive performance with respect to other simplicial complex neural networks.

papers.title: Nonequilibrium Statistical Mechanics: Physical Concepts & Mathematical Tools
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26394v1

summary.background:
- Equilibrium: a state where a system's large-scale properties no longer change over time, as with a cup of coffee reaching room temperature.
- Statistical mechanics: explaining large-scale behavior by averaging over the huge number of tiny particles involved.
- Nonequilibrium: any situation not in such a balanced state, including systems that flow, are driven, or are still relaxing.
- Familiarity with equilibrium statistical mechanics is assumed by the notes.
summary.one_liner: Informal lecture notes introducing core concepts and mathematical tools of classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, assuming prior knowledge of equilibrium statistical mechanics.
summary.plain: These are lecture notes about the physics of systems that are not settled into a steady, balanced state, such as systems that are still changing or are being driven by outside forces. The author says they aim to explain basic ideas and techniques used in this area, and to show how the same tools are applied beyond physics, in fields like biology, ecology, economics, and sociology. The author states that the material is a selection and presentation of known work, with no claim of originality.
summary.why: The text suggests the methods are being used as a common language for complex systems outside physics, which is why the notes may be useful to readers in those fields. The text does not give specific results or examples, so the actual reach of these tools in other fields cannot be judged from this excerpt alone.

papers.abstract: As anything not in equilibrium is, by definition, nonequilibrium, there is no universally agreed-upon set of topics that can constitute an exhaustive presentation of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. At the same time, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics has transcended traditional physics to become a powerful language for complex systems. Prompted by an enthusiastic curiosity about complex systems, these cursory lecture notes attempt to elucidate some introductory concepts and techniques used in classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, which find successful applications not only in foundational physics, but also across other fields such as biology, ecology, economics, and sociology. Except for the specific synthesis and presentation of the material, which assumes basic familiarity with equilibrium statistical mechanics, the author claims no originality.

papers.title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26228v1

summary.background:
- Attention head: a component of a transformer network that learns which other parts of the input to focus on.
- BERT: a widely used pretrained language model based on transformers.
- Phase transition: an abrupt qualitative change in behavior at a critical point, as with water freezing; here, a sudden change as data increases.
- Sample complexity: how much training data is needed to learn something reliably.
- Non-analyticity: a mathematical kink or jump in a smooth curve, which signals a phase transition.
- High-dimensional solvable model: a simplified mathematical model with many parameters whose behavior can be computed exactly in a limit.
- Simplicity bias: a tendency to learn simple features first and more complex ones later.
- Online learning: training on data one example at a time as it arrives.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how attention heads in transformers come to specialize as a function of training-set size rather than training time, showing in a solvable high-dimensional multi-head attention model that specialization appears as a genuine phase transition in sample complexity.
summary.plain: Large language models contain many "attention heads," each of which can end up handling a different job, such as tracking grammar relations. Most prior work has looked at how this specialization unfolds over training time; this paper asks how it depends on how much data the model sees. The authors report that in BERT, heads specialized to syntactic relations appear as the dataset grows, and that in a simplified mathematical model the change is sharp, like a phase change in physics.
summary.why: It reframes head specialization as something governed by how much data is available, not only by training duration, which could inform how much data is needed before internal structure forms. The text does not establish how far these simplified-model results carry over to large real models, so that link remains open.

papers.abstract: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.

papers.title: The phase diagram of fluid hydrogen near melting from machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25178v1

summary.background:
- Hydrogen molecules are pairs of atoms; at high pressure and temperature they can dissociate into single atoms.
- A first-order phase transition is an abrupt change, like ice melting, with a jump in density; it ends at a critical point where the distinction between the two phases disappears.
- A triple point is where three phases (here, two liquids and a solid) coexist.
- Molecular dynamics simulates how atoms move over time; path-integral methods include quantum effects of light nuclei.
- Machine-learned interatomic potentials are fitted models that predict forces between atoms much faster than direct quantum calculations.
- Quantum Monte Carlo is a high-accuracy numerical method for solving the quantum many-body problem; finite-size scaling is a way to locate critical points from simulations of different system sizes.
- Ramp compression is an experimental technique that compresses a sample smoothly over time to high pressure.
summary.one_liner: Classical and quantum path-integral molecular dynamics with two machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo data map the liquid phase diagram of dense hydrogen near melting, reporting a molecular-to-atomic liquid transition, its critical points, and triple points.
summary.plain: This paper studies how hydrogen changes when it is squeezed and heated near its melting point, specifically whether its molecules (pairs of atoms) break apart in a sudden jump or gradually. The authors ran computer simulations using machine-learned models that were trained on very accurate quantum calculations. They report that both models show a sudden, first-order change from molecular liquid to atomic liquid, which ends at critical points, and that triple points lie where this change meets the melting curve.
summary.why: Dense hydrogen matters for planetary interiors such as those of giant planets, and the paper says its predicted triple points should produce clear signatures in ramp-compression experiments. The text does not go further, so the link to specific experiments or planetary models is something a reader should check in the full paper.

papers.abstract: Dissociation of molecular hydrogen increasing temperature or pressure may either occur gradually or abruptly, via a phase transition. Despite considerable experimental and theoretical efforts, the phase diagram of dense hydrogen at temperatures above solid melting is not precisely known. Here, we perform classical and quantum Path Integral molecular dynamics simulations of dense hydrogen using two machine-learned interatomic potentials both trained on quantum Monte Carlo energies and forces. The resulting phase diagram is constructed using state-of-the-art techniques. Both models show a first-order phase transition from the molecular to the atomic liquid terminating in critical points whose locations were determined using finite-size scaling techniques. Triple points, located at the highest temperature of the melting curve, are found at the intersection of the liquid-liquid lines with the melting curve and should lead to clear signatures in ramp compression experiments.

papers.title: A Monte Carlo study of closely packed two-patch particles with frustrated interactions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24560v1

summary.background:
- Patchy particles: particles with localized attractive or repulsive regions (patches) that control how they bond.
- Close packing: particles arranged so that they nearly touch with little empty space, here in two dimensions.
- Frustration: when interactions conflict so no single arrangement can satisfy all of them, often leaving many near-equal lowest-energy states.
- Ground state: the lowest-energy configuration of a system, here found by simulation rather than exact solution.
- Monte Carlo simulation: a computer method that makes random trial changes and accepts them by probabilistic rules to sample configurations.
- Orientational order and nematic order parameter: measures of how aligned particle directions are; disorder means no preferred alignment.
- BKT (Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless) transition: a two-dimensional phase transition involving vortex-like defects, referenced from an earlier paper.
- Correlation decay: how quickly the orientation of one particle stops influencing distant ones; exponential decay means a short correlation length.
summary.one_liner: A Monte Carlo study of closely packed two-patch particles in 2D, showing that competing (frustrated) patch and nonpatch interactions lead to disordered orientational ground states with exponentially decaying correlations.
summary.plain: This paper looks at tiny particles with two sticky spots ("patches") packed tightly on a flat surface, and asks how their orientations arrange themselves. The authors set up interaction rules that pull in competing directions, so the particles cannot satisfy all of them at once. They then used a computer simulation with a special update method to search for the lowest-energy arrangements and found that these arrangements are disordered, with the orientation links fading quickly with distance.
summary.why: It suggests that designing patchy particles could be a way to build orientationally disordered two-dimensional materials, which is a state that is otherwise hard to engineer. The text does not show how far this extends beyond the specific model studied, so its wider relevance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Recently it was found that closely packed two-patch particles exhibit rich orientational ordering behaviors, e.g., nonmonotonic changes of the nematic order parameter and double BKT phase transitions [arXiv:2509.03981]. In this work, we show that, with repulsive patch-patch, attractive patch-nonpatch and intermediate nonpatch-nonpatch interactions, there exist frustrations in the system of closely packed two-patch particles. To investigate the ground states of the system, we design a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm with single-defect propagation. The simulation results show that the ground states are disordered and the correlation functions decay exponentially with the distance. These results demonstrate that in 2D close packing one could design patchy particles to explore orientationally disordered systems.

papers.title: Topological signatures of criticality: the Ising case
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23586v2

summary.background:
- Ising model: a grid of spins, each up or down, with neighbours preferring to align; it has a known ordering transition (ferromagnetic transition) at a specific temperature.
- Order parameter: a quantity, such as net magnetization, that is zero in the disordered phase and nonzero in the ordered phase.
- Euler characteristic: a whole number describing a shape's topology (roughly, number of connected pieces minus number of holes), computed here for cell complexes built from spin regions.
- Monte Carlo simulation with multihistogram reweighting: a computer sampling method that estimates behaviour across nearby temperatures from a set of runs.
- Finite-size scaling: studying systems of different sizes to extract critical temperature and critical exponents, which describe how quantities diverge near the transition.
- Susceptibility: how strongly a quantity responds to a small change in field or temperature; it peaks near a transition.
- Pseudocritical temperature: the finite-size location of such a peak, which approaches the true critical temperature as size grows.
summary.one_liner: A study of the 2D Ising model on square and triangular lattices that defines a spin-odd Euler-characteristic observable from the cell complexes of positive and negative spin domains, relates it to standard Ising quantities, disproves a conjectured lower bound, and uses finite-size scaling to locate the ferromagnetic transition.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a simple magnet model (the Ising model, where tiny spins point up or down on a grid) and asks whether a purely geometric "shape count" of the up-spin and down-spin regions can signal when the magnet loses its ordering as it heats up. The authors build such a count, the Euler characteristic, from the difference between the two kinds of regions, and simulate the model on a computer to test it. They report that this count behaves like an order parameter near the transition and gives estimates of the transition temperature that approach the known value on both grid types.
summary.why: The work tests whether topology, which ignores exact measurements and looks only at connectivity and holes, can locate a phase transition as well as conventional measures. The authors suggest it may help in systems where no standard order parameter can be written down, but the text does not show this beyond the Ising model, and the critical-exponent estimate on the square lattice is reported as sensitive to the fitting range.

papers.abstract: Topological properties of microscopic configurations may provide additional insight into phase transitions beyond conventional thermodynamic observables. We investigate this idea in the two-dimensional Ising model on square and triangular lattices by associating cell complexes with the positive and negative spin domains and constructing an Euler-characteristic observable from their difference. We provide the expression relating this quantity to conventional observables of the Ising model. This derivation allows us to understand its expected behavior physically. As a byproduct, we show that at any finite positive temperature the expectation of the Euler characteristic exceeds a positive, lattice-size-independent bound, hence disproving a previously suggested conjecture. Monte Carlo simulations combined with multihistogram reweighting show that this spin-odd topological observable exhibits order-parameter-like behavior near the ferromagnetic transition. Finite-size scaling of its susceptibility yields pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature for both lattice geometries. On the square lattice, the leading-order estimate of the critical exponent obtained from the topological observable depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate. This behavior is consistent with stronger subleading finite-size corrections, as supported by fits including an additional correction term. On the triangular lattice, the corresponding estimate remains consistent with the theoretical Ising value. Our study suggests that topologically defined quantities such as the Euler characteristic can provide an alternative way to locate order-disorder phase transitions in the systems considered here. Since the definition of these observables is purely geometrical, they can provide useful insights in cases in which order parameters cannot be constructed.

papers.title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23092v1

summary.background:
- Memory kernel: a term in an equation describing how the system's past influences its present.
- Cumulants and moments: statistical summaries of a random quantity; G-cumulants are a specific ordered version used here.
- Boolean cumulants: a particular cumulant type that arises for Poisson (memoryless) switching.
- Renewal process: a sequence of events where waiting times between them are independent and identically distributed.
- Power-law distribution: waiting times with a heavy tail, so very long intervals are not rare; a finite mean means the average waiting time is finite.
- Closure: an approximation that truncates an infinite hierarchy of terms, here at second order.
- Telegraphic process: a signal that switches between two values.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives an exact decomposition of the memory kernel (G-cumulant coefficients) for a controlled variable driven by intermittent random forcing with general renewal waiting times, and studies closure approximations for power-law waiting times with finite mean.
summary.plain: The paper studies systems that are pushed by a signal that changes value only at random moments, holding each value for a random stretch of time. It writes down the exact way past pushes continue to influence the system's future, and shows how this memory simplifies when the waiting times between changes follow a power-law distribution. The authors also give a closed-form approximate equation for the system and test it on a solvable model.
summary.why: Intermittent, switching forcing appears in many physical and control settings, so a clean way to handle its memory could be useful there. The text does not show how widely the results apply beyond the model studied, so the broader significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Many systems are controlled by intermittent control variables that take on a random value for a random time interval. In the presence of such noise at update steps, the main equation for the controlled variables has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the cumulants, also known as $G$-cumulants, of the noise, which are fully ordered in time. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. In the case of waiting times that follow a power-law distribution with a finite mean, it is highly probable that a long time interval will be covered by a single period, and we have shown that, as a result, the coefficients for long delays intersect in all orders, from Boolean cumulants to the usual moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of frozen deterministic flux kernels, weighted by the expression $ξ^2p(ξ)$, and from this the corresponding main equation in closed form follows. For $2<μ<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even in the presence of slow dynamics, whereas the main equation of the frozen flows in this limit yields an exact stationary mean value. The telegraphic process is the only case of noise with renewal steps for which second-order conclusions are exact. An exactly solvable model with additive and correlated multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.

papers.title: When the Boundary Changes the Bulk: Topological Edge Modes in Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19328v1

summary.background:
- Quantum quench: suddenly changing a system's Hamiltonian (its energy rulebook) and watching it evolve.
- Loschmidt amplitude: the overlap between the evolving state and its starting state; its decay rate measures how quickly the system "forgets" its start.
- Dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT): non-analytic kinks in the return rate at certain times, analogous to phase transitions but in time.
- Open chain: a finite one-dimensional chain with ends, where edge modes can localize near the boundary.
- Non-Hermitian matrix: a matrix not equal to its own conjugate transpose; it can have complex eigenvalues and is used here for the Loschmidt matrix.
- Topological classes (A, BDI, AIII, D): the Altland-Zirnbauer tenfold classification of symmetry types; the Z and Z2 labels are integer and parity-type topological invariants.
- Toeplitz operator and K-theory: mathematical tools for counting edge states and index invariants.
- Winding number: a count of how many times a phase rotates around a loop, here in momentum and time.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that edge modes of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix in open-chain dynamical quantum phase transitions are protected by Z and Z2 topological indices (classes A, BDI, AIII, D), with K-splitting theorems giving the bulk-boundary correspondence.
summary.plain: When a quantum system is suddenly switched from one setup to another, its behavior over time can show sharp transitions. In open chains, edge effects at the ends can shift the overall rate at which the system's state "returns" to its starting point. The paper argues that the responsible edge modes are protected by the topology of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix itself, not by the topology of the starting and ending Hamiltonians, and it says these modes can appear even when both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial.
summary.why: It revises the earlier explanation of why boundaries affect bulk behavior in these quench transitions, by moving the source of protection to a different mathematical object. The text does not establish links to applications beyond the theory, and the claims rest on the authors' analysis and numerical data for all four classes.

papers.abstract: For dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in open chains it has been noted that the boundary can change the bulk: in time windows bounded by DQPTs, exponentially localized edge modes of the Loschmidt matrix produce a finite change in the intensive return rate. These modes have been attributed to topological properties of the initial and final Hamiltonians. Here we show that it is not the topology of the Hamiltonians but rather that of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix which protects these edge modes. In particular, we show that topological edge modes can exist in class A, where both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial. For classes A, BDI, and AIII we show that these modes are protected by $\mathbb{Z}$ indices of a Toeplitz operator and that K-splitting theorems provide a precise bulk-boundary correspondence. In class D, they are protected instead by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index that records whether the quench has flipped the fermion parity at the edge. The bulk invariant for class D can be formulated either as a ratio of the Loschmidt amplitudes for periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions or as a winding number that counts phase vortices in momentum and time. We discuss examples and provide numerical data for all four topological classes.

papers.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19848v1

summary.background:
- Language models are neural networks built from stacked layers (a "Transformer"); each layer produces an internal representation of the input text.
- "Representation geometry" refers to the arrangement of these internal vectors in high-dimensional space, such as how spread out or distinguishable they are.
- "Initialization scale" is the size of the random starting weights before training.
- A "phase diagram" is a map showing which regimes a system falls into under different conditions, borrowed from physics.
- A "phase transition" is a sudden qualitative change in a system's behavior, like water freezing.
- A Langevin equation describes motion under a deterministic push plus random noise; "saddle" and "stable node" are types of fixed points describing how trajectories settle or pass by.
- Pythia is a family of openly released language models of different sizes.
summary.one_liner: The paper maps how a language model's internal representation geometry evolves across layers, using two collective coordinates (document distinguishability and document dimension) on a phase diagram, and compares untrained and trained models via a discrete Langevin-style dynamical description.
summary.plain: The paper asks how the hidden internal geometry of a language model, the shape its representations take as text passes through successive layers, relates to how the model actually behaves. The authors summarize each document at each layer with two numbers and plot the path of each document through a "phase diagram," which is a map of regions with different qualitative behavior. They report that untrained models mostly drift toward collapsed or noisy regions, while trained models stay in a central region.
summary.why: It offers a geometric, physics-style way to compare trained and untrained language models, which could help explain why training changes behavior. The text reports only a limited set of models (156 untrained runs, 8 trained models from 5 architecture families, and one case study on Pythia-1.4B), so how far the framing generalizes beyond these is unclear from the text alone.

papers.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.
